questions.q: What makes Preparation different from the other three NIST incident response phases?
options: It's the only phase with no time pressure, happening before any incident occurs
It's the only phase that requires a SIEM
It's the only phase performed exclusively by Tier 1 analysts
It's the only phase that can be skipped without consequence
questions.explain: Preparation happens with no clock running, which is exactly why it's the only phase a team can build deliberately rather than under pressure.

questions.q: Which three categories of work make up real Preparation?
options: A written IR plan, a trained team, and ready tools/access
A SIEM license, a firewall, and an antivirus product
A help desk, a ticketing system, and a wiki
A budget, a vendor contract, and an audit schedule
questions.explain: Lesson 2 defines Preparation as these three things, all of which must exist before an incident starts.

questions.q: What does a real written incident response plan define, according to this lesson?
options: Decision authority for specific actions and severity levels for classifying incidents
Only the names of the SIEM vendors in use
The exact malware signatures the team should expect
A list of every employee's personal contact information with no other content
questions.explain: A real IR plan names who can approve specific actions and defines severity levels, avoiding mid-incident debate.

questions.q: What is a tabletop exercise, as described in this lesson?
options: A simulated incident walkthrough used to train a team without touching production systems
A live attack launched against production to test defenses
A quarterly budget review meeting
A formal certification exam for SOC analysts
questions.explain: Tabletop exercises let a team rehearse the IR plan's steps so they're familiar, not read for the first time during a real incident.

questions.q: An incident starts and the team discovers nobody currently has the admin credentials needed to isolate a compromised server, because the prior admin left and access was never reassigned. According to this lesson, which phase failed?
options: Preparation — ready access should have already been provisioned and verified
Detection & Analysis — the alert should have been triaged faster
Containment, Eradication & Recovery — the server should have been patched
Post-Incident Activity — the review should have caught this earlier
questions.explain: This lesson explicitly calls this a Preparation failure, not a detection problem — the access should have already existed.
